column1: What does food science study?
column2: Food science studies the production, processing, preparing, evaluating, and use of food.

column1: What three qualities does the food industry work to maintain in food from farm gate to plate?
column2: Safe, nutritious, and tasty.

column1: What phrase does the Lesson 01 deck use for the span of the food system that food science covers?
column2: From farm gate to plate - everything from production on the farm through to the food on the consumer's plate.

column1: Name the five sub-fields of food science listed in FNH 200.
column2: Food Chemistry, Food Analysis, Food Microbiology, Food Processing, and Food Engineering.

column1: Which sub-field of food science is described as "structure, composition and properties of foods"?
column2: Food Chemistry (explored in Lessons 2 and 3).

column1: Which sub-field of food science is described as "methods involved in the understanding of food structure"?
column2: Food Analysis (explored in Lesson 2).

column1: Which sub-field of food science is described as "roles of micro-organisms in food borne illness and fermentation"?
column2: Food Microbiology (explored in Lessons 5 and 12).

column1: Which sub-field of food science is described as "manufacturing, packaging, and handling of foods"?
column2: Food Processing (explored in Lessons 6 to 11).

column1: Which sub-field of food science is described as "thermodynamics, energy transfer during the processing of foods"?
column2: Food Engineering (covered only very briefly in FNH 200).

column1: Which single sub-field of food science covers BOTH foodborne illness and fermentation?
column2: Food Microbiology - the same micro-organisms cause illness or are harnessed for fermentation depending on whether they are controlled.

column1: Whose statue stands outside the headquarters of the Institute of Food Technologists (IFT), and what invention does it recognize?
column2: Francois Nicolas Appert, recognized for his invention of canning.

column1: What is the Institute of Food Technologists (IFT)?
column2: An internationally recognized leader in undergraduate education standards for degrees in Food Science; it approves Food Science programs (badge shown: IFT Approved for 2020-2025).

column1: How many essential learning outcomes (ELOs) does IFT establish for approved Food Science programs?
column2: 55 essential learning outcomes.

column1: What does an IFT approval badge on a university program mean?
column2: The program is recognized as delivering a comprehensive Food Science education covering the 55 IFT essential learning outcomes. FNH 200 only begins to introduce some of them.

column1: Which IFT ELO categories are highlighted in the Lesson 01 deck as ones FNH 200 begins to introduce?
column2: Food chemistry (FC), Food microbiology (FM), Sensory science (SS), and Quality assurance (QA) - e.g. FC.1 chemical reactions that limit shelf life; FM.1 beneficial, pathogenic and spoilage microorganisms; SS.1 basis for sensory evaluation; QA.1 defining food quality.

column1: What annual list does the IFT publish?
column2: The Top Ten Food Trends list.

column1: Which Canadian provinces are the major producers of cereal grains?
column2: Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba (the three prairie provinces) - not BC and not Ontario.

column1: What is the typical harvesting month for apples in BC?
column2: October.

column1: What four variables are controlled in controlled atmosphere storage?
column2: Temperature, humidity, oxygen, and carbon dioxide - i.e. "all of the above."

column1: How much oxygen is in the atmosphere (normal air)?
column2: About 21%.

column1: Why is the oxygen level lowered in controlled atmosphere storage of apples?
column2: A harvested apple is still alive and respiring; lowering oxygen, chilling the room and raising CO2 slows its metabolism and ripening so it stays crisp for months.

column1: Why can BC apples be sold in stores in June when they were harvested in October?
column2: Controlled atmosphere storage: sealed rooms with regulated temperature, humidity, oxygen and carbon dioxide slow the fruit's metabolism so one month of harvest supplies twelve months of sales.

column1: In the production of apple cider, what is added to apple juice and what does it yield?
column2: Yeast is added to apple juice and yields ethanol.

column1: Which organism-and-product combination makes vinegar rather than cider?
column2: A bacterial culture producing acetic acid - not yeast producing ethanol. This is the classic distractor pairing on this question.

column1: What value-added product is made from apple juice waste (the pressed-out pulp/pomace)?
column2: Pectin.

column1: What is pectin used for?
column2: It is the gelling agent used to set jams and jellies.

column1: List the five apple products students were asked to rank by processing complexity in the Lesson 01 group activity.
column2: Apple sauce, apple cider, apple juice, an apple from the US, and an apple from New Zealand.

column1: Besides ranking them, what else did the Lesson 01 apple activity ask students to describe?
column2: How the food industry keeps each product fresh - that is, safe, nutritious, and tasty - and the roles of the food industry and food science in doing so.

column1: Why does an imported apple (from the US or New Zealand) add processing complexity?
column2: Distance requires the whole cold chain - storage, shipping and logistics - while still keeping the apple safe, nutritious, and tasty.

column1: Rank these by processing steps: fresh apple, apple sauce, apple juice, apple cider.
column2: Fresh apple (washed, waxed, stored) < apple sauce (chopped, cooked, packed) < apple juice (pressed, filtered, pasteurized) < apple cider (juice plus a biological fermentation step).

column1: What two summary statements does Lesson 01 make about Canada's food system and food industry?
column2: Canada offers a vast and diverse food system, and the Canadian food industry has a strong impact on Canada's economy.

column1: According to the Lesson 01 summary, what has a strong influence on food consumption trends?
column2: Consumers and consumer demands.

column1: According to the Lesson 01 summary, what have technological advancements led to?
column2: Many "food science discoveries."

column1: What image closes Lesson 01 and what point does it make?
column2: Bins of wasted food - a reminder that a large share of what our astonishing food system produces is thrown away.

column1: Which food categories does the Lesson 01 deck use to compare year-over-year changes in availability?
column2: Fresh fruits; fresh vegetables; red meat, poultry, beef and pork; eggs; milk (total, skim, 1%, homo), cheese and cream; wheat flour; and alcohol (beer, wine, spirits).

column1: What is a colloidal dispersion, and what are its two phases?
column2:
A system in which the particles of one substance are distributed (dispersed) in another substance without dissolving.
Dispersed phase = the substance dispersed within another; continuous phase = the substance that extends throughout the system and surrounds it (the exterior/outside).

column1: Table 2.1: a SOLID dispersed in a LIQUID is called what, and what does it do in food?
column2: A sol - e.g. starches, proteins and some plant polysaccharides in water. A sol helps hold small pieces of food suspended in the liquid (e.g. salad dressing).

column1: Table 2.1: a LIQUID dispersed in a LIQUID is called what? Examples?
column2: An emulsion. Examples: milk and mayonnaise.

column1: Table 2.1: a LIQUID dispersed in a SOLID is called what? Examples?
column2: A solid emulsion. Examples: butter and margarine (both are water-in-oil).

column1: Table 2.1: which dispersion is a liquid held in a solid network, and what are its examples?
column2: A gel. Examples: starch, pectin or gelatin gels; also tofu and sausages.

column1: Table 2.1: a GAS dispersed in a LIQUID is called what? Examples?
column2: A foam. Examples: beaten egg white and whipped cake frostings.

column1: Table 2.1: a GAS dispersed in a SOLID is called what? Examples?
column2: A solid foam. Examples: meringue, ice cream and bread. Ice cream must contain at least 36% solids - the rest is largely whipped-in gas.

column1: Which is the MOST accurate description of milk, and how does margarine differ?
column2: Milk is an oil-in-water emulsion (fat droplets dispersed in a continuous water phase). Margarine and butter are the reverse - water-in-oil solid emulsions.

column1: What type of food colloidal dispersion is angel cake or marshmallow?
column2: Solid foam (gas dispersed in a solid).

column1: Why does the fat not float to the top (cream) in commercially available milk?
column2: Each fat droplet is coated by natural milk protein acting as an emulsifier, and the droplets have been made small, so they stay suspended instead of creaming.

column1: Distinguish an emulsifier from a stabilizer, and define creaming.
column2: An emulsifier sits at the oil-water interface and coats the droplets; a stabilizer thickens the continuous phase so droplets cannot rise. Creaming is droplets floating to the top - salad dressings add a stabilizer to prevent it.

column1: What are phospholipids, why are they great emulsifiers, and name the common food example.
column2: Phospholipids are a special fat that is partly water-liking (hydrophilic) and partly oil/fat-liking (hydrophobic), so they sit at the oil-water interface. Lecithin, found in egg yolk and soybean, is the commonly used one.

column1: Name the three carbohydrate classes, the three disaccharides and the enzyme that digests each.
column2:
Monosaccharides (single unit): glucose, fructose, galactose.
Disaccharides: sucrose = glu-fru (invertase), lactose = glu-gal (lactase), maltose = glu-glu (maltase).
Polysaccharides: very long chains of glucose, e.g. starch.

column1: Table 2.2: give the sweetness index of sucrose, fructose, glucose, galactose, maltose and lactose.
column2: Sucrose 100 (the benchmark), fructose (levulose) 140, glucose (dextrose) 70-80, galactose 60, maltose 20, lactose 10-20.

column1: Table 2.2: give the sweetness index of invert sugar, corn syrup, sorbitol, xylitol and the high fructose corn syrups.
column2:
Invert sugar 100-130, corn syrup (glucose/maltose mixture) 50, sorbitol 50, xylitol 100.
HFCS: 42% fructose = 100, 55% fructose = 100+, 90% fructose = 120-160.

column1: Why was the deck's ranking question that included generic 'corn syrup' unanswerable?
column2: It is a tricky question - there is not enough information to determine the ranking, because corn syrup is a variable mixture of glucose and maltose.

column1: Outline the reaction pathway used to make high fructose corn syrup.
column2: Starch (amylose, not sweet) -> amylase or acid -> maltose (slightly sweet) -> maltase -> glucose (sweet) -> glucose isomerase -> fructose (very sweet).

column1: Why is lactose-free milk sweeter than regular milk, and what is invert sugar?
column2: Added lactase splits lactose (index 10-20) into glucose (70-80) and galactose (60), which are sweeter. Invert sugar is sucrose split by invertase or acid into glucose + fructose, giving a sweeter mixture (100-130) than sucrose (100).

column1: In addition to acting as a sweetening agent, what is the primary role of sugar in jam?
column2: Preservative. Sugar binds water, converting free water to bound water so microbes cannot use it.

column1: Contrast the Maillard reaction with caramelization, and name a browning-question item that is neither.
column2: Maillard = sugar AND protein (a reducing sugar plus an amino compound); e.g. bread, toast, coffee, roasted foods. Caramelization = sugar ONLY; e.g. caramel, toffee. Sugar cane is NOT a Maillard product.

column1: What is gelatinization?
column2: What cooking does to starch: starch granules absorb water and swell (e.g. cooking rice or pasta).

column1: What is retrogradation?
column2: The starch recrystallizing so that cooked rice, pasta or bread turns hard again after cooking (e.g. leftovers in the fridge).

column1: What is syneresis, and what are dextrins?
column2: Syneresis is water being squeezed out of a gel (a gel weeping liquid). Dextrins are smaller starch fragments - a term revisited in Lesson 4.

column1: Give the source and food use of pectins, agar and alginates.
column2: Pectins: structural polymers in plants such as apple, the cement between plant cells; gelling agent in jams and jellies, viscosity in tomato paste and ketchup, mouth feel in juice. Agar: extracted from seaweed (kelp), used as a thickener. Alginates: from certain seaweeds, gelling agents that keep solids and liquids suspended in fruit juices.

column1: Give the source and food use of gum arabic, carrageenan and xanthan gum.
column2: Gum arabic (gum acacia): plant exudate from the bark of the acacia tree, thickener and stabilizer. Carrageenan: from certain seaweeds (red algae), suspending agent that keeps cocoa particles suspended in chocolate milk. Xanthan gum: produced by bacteria, first isolated from rotting cabbage, thickener in salad dressings.

column1: List the seven functional roles of fat in food science, and say which one explains deep-fat frying french fries.
column2: Aerate, carry aroma, emulsify, lubricate, soften, tenderize, withstand high temperature. French fries cook quickly because oil can withstand high temperature.

column1: What are the functional roles of proteins in foods, and which milk component makes latte foam?
column2: Proteins act as enzymes and form foams and gels (bread crumb, whipped egg white, cooked egg, sausages, tofu). Milk protein - not milk fat, lactose or other carbohydrate - is responsible for the foam on a latte.

column1: What is the unwelcome role of proteins in foods, and who identifies Canada's list?
column2: Food allergens are proteins. Health Canada and the CFIA identify Canada's priority food allergens: eggs, milk, mustard, peanuts, crustaceans and molluscs, fish, sesame, soy, sulphites, tree nuts and wheat.

column1: What is the most important component in food, and what are the two types of it?
column2: Water. Bound water is bound to food components (salt, sugar, fat, protein) or to the container; free water is available for microbial growth, chemical reactions and enzymatic reactions.

column1: What is water activity, and why can foods not be ranked by moisture content alone?
column2: Water activity (aw) measures the free/available water on a 0 to 1 scale (pure water = 1.0), defined by vapour pressure at equilibrium. Moisture content is not water activity - given apple sauce 95%, fresh egg 75%, fresh meat 72% and apple jelly 35% moisture, you need more data, because the jelly's sugar binds much of its water.

column1: Give the minimum water activity for growth of most bacteria, yeasts and molds, plus the two specialist groups.
column2: Most bacteria aw 0.91, most yeasts aw 0.88, most molds aw 0.80. Osmophilic yeasts go down to aw 0.62 and xerophilic molds to aw 0.65.

column1: List the minor constituents of foods.
column2: Acids, pigments, aroma constituents, vitamins and minerals - present in small amounts but important to food quality and safety.

column1: Name the major acid in apple, and match citric, tartaric and lactic acid to their sources.
column2: Malic acid is the major acid in apple. Citric acid = citrus, tartaric acid = grapes, lactic acid = fermented dairy.

column1: In terms of food safety, which pH is the most critical, and what does it separate?
column2: pH 4.6. A food with pH below 4.6 is low pH / highly acidic (high-acid); a food above pH 4.6 is low-acid.

column1: Which vitamins have additional functions as food additives, and what does calcium sulphate do in tofu?
column2: Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) is a bleaching agent (hastens oxidation and aging as in flour whitening) and a preservative antioxidant that slows rancidity and browning; tocopherols (vitamin E) are preservative antioxidants. Calcium sulphate is the coagulant that sets soy milk into tofu (a gel).

column1: How many Calories per gram does fat provide, and how does that compare to other food components?
column2: Fat provides 9 Cal per gram, making it the most calorie-dense component in food.

column1: Fat substitutes are grouped into which three types, and what is each type classified by?
column2: They are classified by what they are made of: protein-based, carbohydrate-based, and fat-based.

column1: Simplesse: what type of fat substitute is it, what is it made from, and how digestible is it?
column2:
A protein-based fat substitute made from soy, milk or egg white protein.
It is partially digestible.

column1: What is microparticulation?
column2:
The process used to make Simplesse, in which protein is formed into tiny spherical particles.
These protein particles stabilize and give a fat-like creamy texture to food.

column1: How may Simplesse appear in a product's ingredient list?
column2: Products made with Simplesse do NOT have to be labelled "Simplesse"; it may be listed as "modified protein."

column1: Can the fat used to make deep-fried products, such as French fries, be replaced by Simplesse?
column2: No. Simplesse is protein-based and cannot withstand deep-frying; Olean is the fat substitute that can replace deep-frying fat.

column1: Maltrins: what type of fat substitute are they, what are they chemically, and how digestible are they?
column2:
Carbohydrate-based fat substitutes, also called maltodextrins (short chains of starch).
They are fully digestible.

column1: Olean (generic name olestra): what type of fat substitute is it and what is it chemically?
column2: A fat-based fat substitute; chemically it is a combination of "sugar" and "fat."

column1: Olean/olestra: digestibility, calories, and heat behaviour?
column2:
Indigestible, so it contributes no calories.
It is heat stable and can be used for deep-frying (e.g., fat-free Pringles).

column1: Match Simplesse, Maltrin and Olean with indigestible / partially digestible / fully digestible.
column2: Simplesse = partially digestible; Maltrin = fully digestible; Olean = indigestible.

column1: Why is the statement "Vitamins A, D, E and K have been added" needed on products made with olestra?
column2: Because olestra inhibits the absorption of these fat-soluble vitamins, carrying them out of the body as it passes through undigested.

column1: Which olestra-containing products are commercially available in Canada?
column2: None of them. Olestra is not approved in Canada, so no potato chips, low-fat yoghurt or processed meats made with it are sold here.

column1: Under Canada's Food and Drug Regulations, what are sweetening AGENTS and which Division covers them?
column2:
Sweetening agents are the real sugars: honey, sugar and molasses.
They are covered by Division 18.

column1: Under Canada's Food and Drug Regulations, what are sweetenERS and which Division covers them?
column2:
Sweeteners are the sugar substitutes, regulated as food additives.
They are covered by Division 16.

column1: Sugar substitutes fall into which two categories, based on digestibility?
column2: Digestible = low caloric (aspartame, sorbitol); indigestible = non-caloric (cyclamate, sucralose, acesulfame-K).

column1: Aspartame: caloric class, composition, relative sweetness, and required warning (and why)?
column2:
Low caloric (digestible); made of two amino acids; about 200x sweeter than sucrose; carries a PKU warning because people with phenylketonuria cannot metabolize phenylalanine.
It is not heat stable, so it breaks down in baking.

column1: Cyclamate: caloric class and where you would encounter it?
column2: Non-caloric (indigestible) sweetener; it is the sweetener in Sweet'N Low sold in Canada.

column1: Sorbitol: caloric class, chemical family, sweetness, and signature property?
column2:
Low caloric (digestible) sugar alcohol that is LESS sweet than sucrose (sweetness index about 50).
It gives a cooling sensation.

column1: Sucralose: caloric class, relative sweetness, and heat stability?
column2:
Non-caloric (indigestible), about 600x sweeter than sucrose, and heat stable.
It is the sweetener in Splenda, so it can be used in baking.

column1: Acesulfame-K: caloric class, relative sweetness, and heat stability?
column2:
Non-caloric (indigestible), about 200x sweeter than sucrose, and heat stable.
It is often blended with other sweeteners.

column1: Which sugar substitute provides a cool-refreshing sensation in chewing gum, and what is the mechanism?
column2: Sorbitol. Sugar alcohols absorb heat (endothermic) as they dissolve in saliva, so the mouth feels cool.

column1: Name the two plant-derived "natural" sweeteners covered in Lesson 3.
column2: Stevia (from a plant leaf) and monk fruit.

column1: On the relative sweetness index, what is the reference value, and what are the values for fructose, glucose, maltose, lactose, sorbitol and xylitol?
column2:
Sucrose = 100 is the reference.
Fructose 140, glucose (dextrose) 70-80, maltose 20, lactose 10-20, sorbitol 50, xylitol 100.

column1: What is the enzymatic sequence that converts starch into progressively sweeter sugars?
column2: Starch (amylose, not sweet) --amylase or acid--> maltose (slightly sweet) --maltase--> glucose (sweet) --glucose isomerase--> fructose (very sweet).

column1: How does the Food and Drug Regulations table of "Food Additives That May Be Used as Sweeteners" (Table IX) control each sweetener?
column2:
It lists each additive with the foods it is permitted in or on and the maximum level of use.
Example: acesulfame-potassium is allowed at 0.35% in chewing gum and 0.025% in carbonated beverages as consumed.

column1: What are the three sensory factors that determine whether a food is good (yummy)?
column2: Appearance, texture and flavour — where flavour includes aroma and taste.

column1: Food texture is measured as which four mechanical forces?
column2: Compression, cutting, shearing and tensile strength.

column1: How do we describe the force needed to squeeze a loaf of bread?
column2: Compression.

column1: How do we perceive aroma?
column2: Fat-soluble volatiles interacting with receptors in our nasal passages.

column1: How do we perceive taste, and what are the tastes?
column2:
Water-soluble compounds interacting with receptors on the tongue (taste buds).
Four classic tastes — sweet, sour, salty, bitter — plus the fifth, umami (savoury).

column1: What is MSG and what does it do?
column2:
Monosodium glutamate, a flavour enhancer.
It enhances savoury (umami) character and suppresses bitterness.

column1: Match the oral sensations astringency, pungency and coolness with the molecules responsible.
column2: Astringency = tannins; pungency = capsaicin; coolness = xylitol.

column1: Which oral sensation is caused by tannins, and where would you encounter it?
column2: Astringency — the dry, puckery mouthfeel of red wine or strong tea.

column1: Name the three common sensory evaluation tests and what each one measures.
column2: Hedonic test (consumers, how much they like it); discriminative test, a.k.a. difference test (can two products be told apart); descriptive test (trained panel, detailed product profile).

column1: Which sensory test measures consumer acceptance level of a new product, and which offers the most details during product development?
column2:
Consumer acceptance level = hedonic test.
Most details during product development = descriptive analysis.

column1: What is the Food and Drugs Act, in full?
column2: R.S.C., 1985, c. F-27 — "An Act respecting food, drugs, cosmetics and therapeutic devices." It is the foundational federal food law in Canada.

column1: Food and Drugs Act Section 3 — what does it prohibit, and for which diseases?
column2:
Advertising any food, drug, cosmetic or device to the general public as a treatment, preventative or cure for a Schedule A disease; 3(2) also bans selling a product represented that way.
Schedule A includes alcoholism, appendicitis, arthritis, cancer, depression, diabetes, heart disease, hypertension, liver diseases, obesity, sexual impotence, tumours, venereal disease.

column1: Food and Drugs Act Section 4 — what does it prohibit?
column2: No person shall SELL an article of food that: has a poisonous or harmful substance; is unfit for human consumption; consists of any filthy, putrid, disgusting, rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or vegetable substance; is adulterated; or was manufactured, prepared, preserved, packaged or stored under unsanitary conditions.

column1: Food and Drugs Act Section 5 — what does it prohibit?
column2:
5(1): no labelling, packaging, treating, processing, selling or advertising of food that is false, misleading or deceptive, or likely to create an erroneous impression regarding character, value, quantity, composition, merit or safety.
5(2): food not labelled or packaged as the regulations require is deemed contrary to 5(1).

column1: Food and Drugs Act Section 7 — what does it prohibit?
column2: No person shall manufacture, prepare, preserve, package or store for sale any food under unsanitary conditions.

column1: What is the key difference between Section 4 and Section 7 of the Food and Drugs Act?
column2: Section 4 is about SELLING food that is itself harmful, unfit, putrid or adulterated. Section 7 is about the unsanitary CONDITIONS under which food is made, packaged or stored for sale.

column1: Which agency administers the Food and Drugs Act, and what are its regulatory functions?
column2: Health Canada, Health Products and Food Branch (HPFB). It sets standards of identity and composition for foods, administers the Food and Drugs Act, and writes the food additive regulations.

column1: Which agency enforces the Food and Drugs Act, and what are its regulatory functions?
column2: The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA). It provides food inspection services, enforces Acts including the Food and Drugs Act and the Agriculture and Agri-Food Administrative Monetary Penalties Act, and handles food labelling for industry — so accurate labelling is CFIA's responsibility.

column1: Which agency approves food additives such as aspartame and nitrites?
column2: Health Canada — additive approval is administration and rule-setting, not enforcement, so it is not CFIA.

column1: What are the six pieces of information mandatory on every food label in Canada?
column2: 1) Bilingual (English and French); 2) common name; 3) net quantity; 4) name of the business; 5) ingredient list; 6) Nutrition Facts table — all legible, with placement rules.

column1: What label information is required only DEPENDING ON THE FOOD (conditional, not universal)?
column2: Best before date, country of origin, sweeteners such as aspartame, irradiated foods, % milk fat and % alcohol, and allergens.

column1: Of net quantity, % milk fat, % alcohol, Nutrition Facts and ingredient list, which is NOT mandatory on a yogurt label?
column2: % alcohol — it is conditional and applies to alcoholic beverages. % milk fat IS mandatory on yogurt because yogurt is a dairy product.

column1: How many disease risk reduction claims are approved in Canada, and how do they square with Section 3?
column2: Five. Section 3 bans treatment, preventative or CURE claims for Schedule A diseases, but this short approved list of RISK REDUCTION claims is permitted.

column1: Name the five approved disease risk reduction claims in Canada.
column2: 1) Sodium and potassium; 2) calcium and vitamin D; 3) saturated and trans fats; 4) cancer risk reduction; 5) dental caries.

column1: What is the front-of-package (FOP) label in Canada?
column2: A black-and-white magnifying-glass symbol from Health Canada reading "High in / Élevé en," flagging foods high in saturated fat, sugars, and/or sodium on the front of the package.

column1: What is a standardized food, and what are some examples?
column2:
A food for which the Food and Drug Regulations prescribe a standard of identity — WHAT must be in it and HOW MUCH.
Standardized: bread, enriched white bread, raisin bread, whole wheat bread, ice cream. Not standardized: pizza dough.

column1: Why can a fat-free frozen product not be called "ice cream" in Canada?
column2: Ice cream is a standardized food with a required minimum milk fat content. A product lacking that milk fat must be renamed — hence "frozen dessert."

column1: Name the grades of eggs in Canada.
column2: Canada Grade A, Grade B, Grade C, and Nest Run. Canada Fancy and Canada Choice are NOT egg grades.

column1: Name the grades for processed fruit such as canned peaches, and does brand predict grade?
column2: Canada Fancy, Canada Choice, Canada Standard. Grade is independent of brand — in the class demo a no-name peach product was Canada Fancy while a competing can was Canada Choice.

column1: Name the grades of beef in Canada and what distinguishes them.
column2: Canada A, AA, AAA, and Prime — increasing marbling (fat within the muscle). Canada A requires only that some marbling be visible; Prime is the most marbled.

column1: Roughly how many food additives are approved in Canada versus the United States, and why the difference?
column2: Roughly 300 in Canada versus over 2,600 in the US. The gap is due mainly to differences in the DEFINITION of a food additive, not to different chemicals in the food supply.

column1: What five categories does Canada's definition of "food additive" exclude?
column2: Nutritive materials, seasonings, agricultural residues, food packaging materials, and drugs for therapeutic uses in animals (veterinary drugs).

column1: What is Division 16 of the Food and Drug Regulations?
column2: The tables of permitted food additives, listing for each additive the foods it is permitted in or upon and the maximum level of use and other conditions. Approval is therefore use-specific and level-specific, never general.

column1: What must be submitted to Health Canada to get a new food additive approved?
column2: Composition, properties and method of manufacture; amount and purpose of use; method of analysis; data on intended physical or other technical effect; detailed reporting of tests; a proposed maximum residue limit in the finished food; specimens of the labelling; and a sample of the additive.

column1: Describe the dose-response curve, and how do common foods differ from poisons on it?
column2: Regions: a flat "no effect" zone, a threshold, a dose range of increasing response, then a plateau at maximum effect. Everything has a curve — even common foods — but poisons have a far lower threshold.

column1: What is the Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI)?
column2: The amount of an additive that can safely be consumed daily over a lifetime, derived from the no-effect level for humans on the dose-response curve with safety margins applied.

column1: What is the Probable Daily Intake (PDI)?
column2: The amount of an additive people are actually likely to consume, estimated from real dietary patterns. It must sit well below the ADI.

column1: What happens when the probable daily intake of an additive exceeds the acceptable daily intake?
column2: The additive will not be approved, or will be approved only with restricted use.

column1: Aspartame: who is it for, who must avoid it, and what does it break down into on digestion?
column2: Intended for people with diabetic concerns; people with phenylketonuria (PKU) must avoid it, hence the phenylalanine warning. Digestion yields aspartic acid, methanol, and phenylalanine.

column1: How much aspartame is in a can of diet pop, how many cans reach the ADI, and where does that intake sit on the dose-response curve?
column2: About 200 mg per can, and about 12 cans per day would be needed to reach the ADI. Actual probable daily intake sits far to the left, deep in the flat no-effect region.

column1: Why are nitrites used in cured meats?
column2: All of the above: to develop the pink colour of the finished product, to enhance flavour (meat + nitrite + salt + heat gives cured meat flavour), and to act as an antimicrobial agent.

column1: What is the colour chemistry of cured versus ordinary cooked meat?
column2: Myoglobin (red) + heat gives metmyoglobin (brown). Myoglobin (red) + nitrite (NO2-) gives nitrosylhemochrome, the stable pink of cured ham.

column1: How does nitrite act as an antimicrobial in cured meats?
column2: Nitrite prevents spores of Clostridium botulinum from germinating into growing, toxin-producing cells.

column1: Which chemical found in cured meat is potentially carcinogenic, and how is it formed?
column2: Nitrosamines — formed by nitrite + amines with heat. Not nitrates, nitrites, nitric oxide, or nitrosylhemochrome.

column1: Despite the risk, why is nitrite still approved for cured meat in Canada?
column2: All of the above: foods are not a major source of nitrosamine exposure; the risk appears to be very low; and no suitable replacement has been identified to control Clostridium botulinum.

column1: List the eight causes of food deterioration shown in the Lesson 5 diagram.
column2:
1. Microorganisms (bacteria, yeasts, moulds)
2. Food enzymes and other chemical reactions within the food itself
3. Reaction with oxygen and/or light
4. Gain or loss of moisture
5. Inappropriate temperatures
6. Time
7. Physical stress or abuse
8. Infestation by insects, parasites, and rodents

column1: Food deterioration causes are grouped into which three broad categories?
column2: Physical, chemical, or biological causes.

column1: What are the three primary goals of food preservation?
column2: To keep food safe, nutritious, and of good quality.

column1: True or false: a good preservation method can completely eliminate spoilage.
column2: False. No method can completely eliminate spoilage; preservation only slows deterioration down.

column1: Which three types of factors contribute to food deterioration and spoilage (Lesson 5 learning objective)?
column2: Chemical, enzymatic, and microbiological factors.

column1: Which microorganism is the MOST resistant in a normal environment?
column2: Bacterial spores. Clostridium botulinum is the named example.

column1: Rank the four microorganism types from least to most resistant in a normal environment.
column2: Vegetative cells of bacteria (least) to yeasts to moulds to bacterial spores (most resistant).

column1: How does the lecture describe vegetative cells of bacteria?
column2: Most common, active, and alive. They are the least resistant of the four microorganism types.

column1: How does the lecture describe yeasts?
column2: They survive in less ideal environments and are involved in fermentation.

column1: How does the lecture describe moulds?
column2: They tolerate a wide range of environments, pH, and water activity (Aw).

column1: Which named organism is the lecture example of a bacterial spore former?
column2: Clostridium botulinum.

column1: Name the three classifications of microorganisms based on oxygen requirement.
column2: Aerobic (need oxygen), anaerobic (grow without oxygen), and facultative anaerobe (grow either way).

column1: What types of bacteria can grow in canned food?
column2: Anaerobic and facultative anaerobic bacteria. Aerobes cannot, because a sealed can has no oxygen.

column1: What is the growth temperature range of psychrophiles?
column2: 0 to 18 degrees C.

column1: What is the growth temperature range of psychrotrophs?
column2: -5 to 35 degrees C.

column1: What is the growth temperature range of mesophiles?
column2: 10 to 45 degrees C.

column1: What is the growth temperature range of thermophiles?
column2: 50 to greater than 100 degrees C.

column1: Which microorganisms are responsible for most spoilage in refrigerated foods?
column2: Psychrotrophs (-5 to 35 degrees C), not psychrophiles. Their wide range lets them grow at fridge temperatures and quickly at room temperature.

column1: What is the difference between a psychrophile and a psychrotroph?
column2: Psychrophiles are cold specialists growing 0 to 18 degrees C; psychrotrophs are cold-tolerant generalists growing -5 to 35 degrees C.

column1: In the GOOD, BAD, and UGLY scheme, what are the GOOD microorganisms?
column2: Those involved in fermentation.

column1: In the GOOD, BAD, and UGLY scheme, what are the BAD microorganisms?
column2: Those that spoil our foods.

column1: In the GOOD, BAD, and UGLY scheme, what are the UGLY microorganisms?
column2: Those that cause foodborne illnesses. They often do not change the taste or smell of the food.

column1: Which microorganism types may contribute to fermentation?
column2: Vegetative cells of bacteria, yeasts, and moulds. Bacterial spores do NOT contribute to fermentation.

column1: Give the lecture example of one organism type being both GOOD and UGLY.
column2: Moulds: the white rind on brie is good, but mould growing on bread is not. Context determines the category.

column1: Which organisms cause deterioration by infestation?
column2: Insects, parasites, and rodents, plus birds (the lecture adds crows).

column1: Name the enzyme responsible for the browning of an apple after it is cut.
column2: Polyphenol oxidase. It oxidizes phenolic compounds into brown pigments, causing enzymatic browning.

column1: How does enzymatic browning differ from Maillard browning and caramelization?
column2: Enzymatic browning is a separate third browning pathway driven by polyphenol oxidase plus oxygen, not by sugar plus protein (Maillard) or sugar plus heat (caramelization).

column1: List four ways to prevent apple slices from enzymatic browning.
column2: Dipping in hot water, dipping in water, dipping in water with lemon juice, and applying sulfur dioxide (all of the above).

column1: Why does each browning-prevention method work: hot water, plain water, lemon juice, sulfur dioxide?
column2: Hot water denatures the enzyme; plain water blocks oxygen; lemon juice lowers the pH below the enzyme's working range; sulfur dioxide is a chemical inhibitor.

column1: An uncut apple is brown on the inside. What caused the colour change?
column2: Improper storage temperature. It is a storage injury, not sunlight, moisture loss, or parasite infestation.

column1: What combination of components causes oxidation and lipolytic rancidity?
column2: Fat and oxygen.

column1: Give lecture examples of physical damage as a cause of deterioration.
column2: Crushing of fresh fruits, cookies, and similar products.

column1: Retrogradation of bread starch leads to tough and dry bread due to what?
column2: All of: syneresis squeezing water out from between the starch molecules, moisture loss during storage, and exclusion of the water previously absorbed during gelatinization.

column1: Give examples of semi-perishable foods.
column2: Ice cream, cheese, and potato chips. Dehydrated pasta is NOT semi-perishable, it is shelf stable.

column1: Give examples of perishable and shelf-stable foods.
column2: Perishable (days): fresh meat, fish, milk, soft produce. Shelf stable (months to years): canned goods, sugar, flour, dehydrated pasta.

column1: What thermal process is used when apple slices are dipped in hot water to prevent enzymatic browning, and what does it target?
column2: Blanching, a mild heat treatment that inactivates enzymes such as polyphenol oxidase. It is also what is done to vegetables before freezing.

column1: What is the main purpose of pasteurizing milk?
column2: To eliminate pathogenic (ugly) microorganisms. It does not target spoilage organisms, psychrotrophs, or enzymes, which is why pasteurized milk still spoils and needs refrigeration.

column1: What does commercial sterilization aim for, and which organism is it aimed at?
column2: It aims for 'complete' elimination of all microorganisms, targeting Clostridium botulinum spores. It is achieved by canning and UHT (ultra-high temperature).

column1: Which of these does commercial sterilization target: spoilage organisms, pathogens, spores, thermophilic spores? Why are thermophilic spores excluded?
column2: It targets spoilage-causing microorganisms, pathogenic microorganisms and spores, but NOT thermophilic spores. Thermophiles need about 50 C or more to grow, so survivors sit harmlessly at storage temperature - hence commercial rather than absolute sterility.

column1: Canning vs UHT: what is the difference in the order of operations?
column2: Canning: food is placed in the container and sealed FIRST, then the whole package is heated. UHT: the food is heated up first at ultra-high temperature, THEN filled into the container.

column1: Do the containers have to be sterilized before filling in canning vs in UHT?
column2: Canning containers only need to be clean, because the sealed package is heated afterwards. UHT containers must be fully sterilized beforehand.

column1: What is aseptic packaging?
column2: The food and the package are sterilized separately and then combined (filled and sealed) in a sterile environment. It is what makes UHT products shelf-stable.

column1: What is the official name of the juice-box packaging material, and how is it most commonly sterilized?
column2: Tetra Pak, sterilized with hydrogen peroxide. Not ascorbic acid, carbon dioxide, pressurized steam, or superheated steam.

column1: Give examples of canned products vs UHT-aseptically packaged products.
column2: Canning: SPAM, canned tuna, soup, canned peaches. UHT-aseptic: shelf-stable Parmalat milk (longest shelf life of the milks shown), ketchup, sriracha, protein shakes, latte pouches.

column1: Packaging pros and cons: tin can and glass jar.
column2: Tin can: durable, cheap, opaque, but heavy and can corrode. Glass jar: inert, resealable, see-through, but heavy and breakable.

column1: Packaging pros and cons: Tetra Pak and retortable pouch.
column2: Tetra Pak: light and cheap to ship, but not resealable and hard to recycle. Retortable pouch: light and heats fast, but can puncture.

column1: Choosing between blanching, pasteurization and sterilization depends on what three things?
column2: The type of food (chemical, taste, usage), the storage conditions, and the targeted microorganisms.

column1: How do you recognize a logarithmic graph, and why is one used for survivor counts?
column2: Its gridlines bunch up and are labelled in powers of ten (1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000) instead of even intervals (0, 10, 20, 30...). Each heating interval kills the same percentage, not the same number (6000 to 600 to 60 to 6), so a log axis turns survivors vs time into a straight line.

column1: Distinguish the thermal death RATE curve from the thermal death TIME curve.
column2: Thermal death rate curve: number of survivors (log scale) vs time at one temperature; its slope gives the D-value. Thermal death time curve: D-value (log scale) vs temperature; it gives the Z-value.

column1: Define the D-value, and state when it stays constant.
column2: D-value (decimal reduction time) is the time it takes to kill 90% of the microorganisms, i.e. one log cycle. It is fixed for the same microorganism, in the same food, at the same temperature - but it changes at different processing temperatures.

column1: On thermal death rate curves, how does the slope relate to the D-value, and which organisms are most resistant?
column2: Steeper line = faster death = smaller D-value, so the shallowest line (e.g. C among A, B, C) has the largest D-value. Ranked by resistance: vegetative cells (steepest) < C. botulinum spores < spores of thermophilic bacteria (shallowest).

column1: Starting with 6000 microbes and D = 5 min, list the survivors at 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 and 25 minutes.
column2:
6000, 600, 60, 6, 0.6, 0.06.
One log cycle is removed every 5 minutes.

column1: Chicken broth (pH 6.2) had 4,000 units of bacteria; after 18 min at 98 C only 4 units were left. What is the D-value?
column2:
4000 -> 400 -> 40 -> 4 = 3 log cycles.
D = 18 min / 3 = 6 minutes.

column1: Chicken broth, pH 6.2, D = 6 min. According to common practice, how long should it be processed?
column2:
pH 6.2 is at or above 4.6, so it is low-acid -> 12D.
12 x 6 min = 72 minutes.

column1: A pathogen has a decimal reduction time of 5 minutes in tomato juice at 91 C. How long should the juice (pH 3.8) be processed to sterilize it?
column2:
pH 3.8 is below 4.6, so it is high-acid -> 5D.
5 x 5 min = 25 minutes.

column1: Bacterial load fell from 40,000 to 4,000 units in 4 minutes. Find D, and the total time for (i) 4 units, (ii) 0.4 units, (iii) 5D, (iv) 12D.
column2:
40,000 -> 4,000 is 1 log cycle in 4 min, so D = 4 min.
(i) 4 logs = 16 min; (ii) 5 logs = 20 min
(iii) 5D = 20 min; (iv) 12D = 48 min.

column1: State the pH 4.6 rule for processing time.
column2: pH equal to or above 4.6 (low-acid): longer processing time, 12D (12 times the D-value). pH below 4.6 (high-acid): shorter processing time, 5D (5 times the D-value).

column1: What is the '12D botulinum cook' and why is it considered enough?
column2: Twelve log reductions of C. botulinum in low-acid food. Starting from one spore per can, the odds of a survivor are about one in a trillion, giving safety without ever having to prove sterility.

column1: Define the Z-value, and say what a small Z-value implies.
column2: Z-value is the change in temperature that causes a 10x change (one log cycle) in the D-value. A small Z-value means the organism is very responsive to temperature.

column1: A pathogen has D = 5 min (300 s) at 91 C and Z = 5 C. What is its D-value at 121 C?
Tomato juice: D = 7 min (420 s) at 91 C, Z = 5 C. Give D at 96, 101, 106, 111, 116 and 121 C.
column2:
Every 5 C rise divides D by 10.
42, 4.2, 0.42, 0.042, 0.0042, 0.00042 seconds.

column1: Tomato juice at pH 4.4 has D = 0.00042 s at 121 C. What is the F-value?
column2:
pH 4.4 is below 4.6, so high-acid -> 5D.
F = 5 x 0.00042 = 0.0021 seconds.

column1: Pineapple juice heated at 96 C for 30 min: Bacteria A went 48,000 -> 4,800 (Z = 10 C), Bacteria B went 150,000 -> 150 (Z = 5 C). Find their D-values at 96, 106 and 86 C.
column2:
A: 1 log in 30 min -> D = 30 min; at 106 C = 3 min; at 86 C = 300 min.
B: 3 logs in 30 min -> D = 10 min; at 106 C (10/5 = 2 cycles) = 0.1 min; at 86 C = 1000 min.

column1: Define the F-value.
column2: A mathematically calculated number describing the total lethal effect of the process at the slowest heating point in the container. It is the time required to sterilize a selected organism at the reference temperature 121.1 C (250 F).

column1: What are the three steps for calculating an F-value?
column2: 1) Convert the D-value to 121 C using the Z-value. 2) Check the pH of the food to decide 5D or 12D. 3) Multiply. Convert first, then decide 5D or 12D.

column1: Ranch dressing, pH 5.3, D = 3 min (180 s) at 91 C, Z = 10 C. What is the F-value?
column2:
30 C / 10 = 3 log cycles, so 180 s -> 0.18 s at 121 C.
pH 5.3 is above 4.6 -> 12D; F = 12 x 0.18 = 2.16 seconds.

column1: What assumptions and precautions create the margin of safety in thermal processing?
column2: Assume the most commonly found toxic microorganism C. botulinum is present, assume it is in its most resistant form (spores), and design the process on an even more heat-resistant relative. Plus: C. botulinum does not grow in acid, and sanitation minimizes the starting contamination.

column1: Conduction heating: how does heat move, in which foods, and where is the cold point?
column2: Heat transfers molecule to molecule in straight lines, in solid foods such as SPAM and pumpkin puree. The cold point is at the geometric centre of the container.

column1: Convection heating: how does heat move, in which foods, and where is the cold point?
column2: Heat transfers by fluid motion - the fluid heats along the hot container walls and rises - in thin liquids such as broth and juice. It is much faster and the cold point sits lower, below the centre.

column1: How is heat transferred in a can of corn chowder, and what about cranberry sauce that gels during processing?
column2: Corn chowder: mainly convection, with some conduction. Cranberry sauce starts as a liquid heated by convection and gels partway through, switching to conduction.

column1: What is the temperature range used for cold storage (refrigeration) of foods?
column2: -2 to 16 degrees C.

column1: What does cold storage / refrigeration do to microorganisms?
column2: It slows down the growth of microorganisms. It does not stop growth and does not kill them.

column1: Is there a single optimal refrigeration temperature for all foods?
column2: No. The optimal temperature varies by food, and some produce is actually damaged at refrigeration temperatures.

column1: Freezing preserves foods by which three mechanisms?
column2: Slowing down microbial growth, stopping microbial growth, and freezing water molecules.

column1: Does freezing kill and eliminate microorganisms?
column2: No. Freezing does NOT kill microorganisms; it freezes water, and the dormant microbes resume growing on thawing.

column1: What happens to water activity when a food is frozen?
column2: It decreases. Liquid water is converted to ice, so free water available to microorganisms drops (freezing does NOT increase water activity).

column1: What is modified atmosphere packaging (MAP)?
column2: The gas mixture inside the package is altered at the time of packing and then left alone. Examples: trays of salami, pre-cut fruit, fresh pasta.

column1: What is controlled atmosphere packaging/storage?
column2: Storage conditions (the gas atmosphere) are actively monitored and maintained over time, as in commercial apple storage rooms.

column1: What is vacuum packaging, and which microorganisms is it especially effective against?
column2: Air is drawn out of the package before sealing. It is especially effective against aerobic spoilage-causing bacteria.

column1: What does vacuum packaging NOT protect against?
column2: Anaerobic organisms. This is why vacuum-packed deli meats still need nitrite and refrigeration.

column1: What is moisture barrier packaging?
column2: Packaging designed to keep water in the food or keep water out of the food.

column1: What is syneresis, and which refrigerated-food changes does it cause?
column2: Syneresis is water being squeezed out of a gel network. In refrigerated foods it causes staling of bread and drip loss in fish.

column1: Which refrigerated-food changes are NOT caused by syneresis?
column2: Colour change in fresh meat (that is pigment chemistry), loss of nutrients, and loss of crispness and flavour in fruits and vegetables.

column1: During freezing, what happens to the volume of water, and why does it matter?
column2: It increases; water expands about 9% as it becomes ice. The expanding ice crystals push against, stretch, and can puncture cell walls.

column1: Rapid (deep) freezing produces what kind of ice crystals, and where?
column2: Many small ice crystals, formed both inside and outside the cells, causing minimal structural damage.

column1: Slow (mild-temperature) freezing produces what kind of ice crystals, and where?
column2: Few large ice crystals, formed mostly outside the cells; they grow large and rupture cell walls, giving mushy thawed product.

column1: What is drip loss?
column2: Loss of cell fluid from a thawed food because large ice crystals ruptured the cell structure during freezing or frozen storage.

column1: Drip loss in thawed strawberries is a result of what?
column2: The formation of large ice crystals due to fluctuating storage temperature.

column1: What is the single most important factor in producing high-quality frozen foods?
column2: Keeping the freezing/storage temperature CONSTANT (not simply keeping it low, and not crystal size alone).

column1: What is recrystallization in frozen foods?
column2: When storage temperature fluctuates, ice partly melts and refreezes elsewhere, so water molecules migrate and join existing crystals, which grow larger.

column1: Ice crystals seen on improperly stored ice cream are a result of what?
column2: Migration of water molecules, caused by fluctuating (not stable) storage temperature.

column1: What is freeze burn?
column2: The dried, discoloured, leathery patches seen on improperly packaged frozen foods such as meat and chicken.

column1: What physical process causes freeze burn?
column2: Sublimation: ice passes directly to vapour and escapes through inadequate packaging, leaving dehydrated tissue behind.

column1: Name the four freezing methods covered in Lesson 7.
column2: Air-blast freezing, indirect contact freezing, immersion freezing, and cryogenic freezing.

column1: What is air-blast freezing, and what specialized equipment does it include?
column2: Cold air is blasted over the food. It includes fluidized-bed freezers, which produce IQF (individually quick frozen) product such as small pieces and chunks.

column1: Strawberries, mango chunks and shrimp are best frozen by which method?
column2: Individually quick frozen (IQF) by fluidized-bed freezers.

column1: What is indirect contact freezing, and what equipment is used?
column2: The food contacts a cold surface but never touches the refrigerant itself. Equipment includes plate freezers and slush freezers.

column1: What is immersion freezing?
column2: The food, usually already packaged, is dunked into a cold liquid; contact is excellent so freezing is very fast.

column1: A turkey (or other large, bagged, irregular food) is frozen by which method?
column2: Immersion freezing.

column1: What is cryogenic freezing?
column2: The extreme, near-instant freezing method, using liquid nitrogen or carbon dioxide.

column1: Which packaging material is NOT suitable for frozen products, and why?
column2: Glass bottles. Water expands on freezing but glass does not, so the glass shatters.

column1: Which packaging materials are standard versus less common for frozen foods?
column2: Standard: cardbox (cardboard) and plastic film. Less common but workable: foil film and Tetra Pak.

column1: How does thawing rate compare with freezing rate, and why?
column2: Thawing is slower than freezing. Water conducts heat better than ice, so the thawed outer layer insulates the still-frozen core.

column1: Why should frozen food be thawed in the refrigerator rather than on the counter?
column2: The warm thawed outer layer is ideal for microbial growth, and freezing never killed those microbes - it only paused them.

column1: Rank the shelf life of pasteurized milk (jug or carton) versus UHT-sterilized Parmalat milk.
column2: UHT-sterilized Parmalat is longest (months, shelf-stable without refrigeration); pasteurized milk plus refrigeration is shortest (days).

column1: What is the principle of dehydration?
column2: Removal of free water AND lowering of water activity. It is NOT elimination of pathogenic or spoilage-causing microorganisms.

column1: Does dehydration kill or eliminate microorganisms in food?
column2: No. Drying only lowers water activity so microbes cannot grow - like freezing, which immobilizes free water as ice instead of removing it. Pathogens and spoilage organisms survive and grow again once the food is rehydrated and held warm.

column1: During dehydration, what happens to water in the food? (exam wording)
column2: It is removed from the surface of the food first, AND it is often trapped in the centre. Both statements are true.

column1: What is case hardening?
column2: When the surface dries too fast it forms a tough, sealed shell while the inside is still wet, so trapped moisture cannot escape. The result is a leathery crust around a damp core - unstable and prone to spoiling from within.

column1: How is case hardening prevented?
column2: Dry gently: lower temperature and longer drying time, so the moisture gradient stays manageable.

column1: What is the white powder seen on the surface of dried pineapple or mango?
column2: Sugar.

column1: How does the white sugar powder get onto the surface of dried pineapple?
column2: It was left behind on the surface as water was removed. It was not added; water evaporates but dissolved sugar cannot, so it crystallizes out on the surface.

column1: Name the seven dehydration methods covered in Lesson 08.
column2: Sun drying, tray (hot air) drying, spray drying, vacuum microwave drying, drum drying, deep fat frying, extrusion drying.

column1: What is the most common form of dehydration worldwide?
column2: Sun drying.

column1: Why is sun drying so widely used, and what does it require?
column2: It is the oldest method, cheap and needs no equipment; it does require good weather.

column1: Give signature foods dried by sun drying.
column2: Raisins, dried shiitake mushrooms, dried mango.

column1: Describe tray (hot air) drying.
column2: Food is placed on trays and hot air is blown over it. Simple and industrial, but the heat damages colour and flavour.

column1: Describe how spray drying works.
column2: A liquid is atomized into a fine mist inside a hot chamber; the tiny droplets dry almost instantly and fall out as a powder.

column1: Skim milk powder, instant coffee, and other liquid foods are often dried by which method?
column2: Spray drying. Exam shortcut: if the question says liquid turned into a powder, the answer is spray drying.

column1: Describe how drum drying works.
column2: A slurry is spread as a thin film on a hot rotating drum heated by 120 degrees C steam inside; the thin dry layer is scraped off and falls into a solids collector.

column1: What is a doctor blade and where is it used?
column2: The blade in a drum drier that scrapes the thin dried sheet off the surface of the rotating drum.

column1: What is the signature product of drum drying?
column2: Instant mashed potato (potato slurry dried to flakes).

column1: Which dehydration technique was developed at UBC?
column2: Vacuum microwave drying.

column1: How does vacuum microwave drying work and why is it good?
column2: Microwaves heat the food from within while a vacuum lets water boil off at low temperature. It is fast and gentle, so colour and nutrients are retained.

column1: In deep fat frying, which functional property of fat (from Lesson 02) makes it work as a drying medium?
column2: Fat withstands high temperature. The hot oil flashes the water out of the food.

column1: What is the important property of deep fat-fried instant noodles?
column2: Rapid rehydration rate due to the voids left as water evaporated. Escaping steam leaves a sponge of tiny channels that boiling water floods back into.

column1: Describe extrusion drying.
column2: Dough is forced under heat and pressure through a die; when it exits into normal pressure the trapped steam flashes off and the product puffs.

column1: Give signature foods made by extrusion drying.
column2: Cheerios, cheese puffs, shrimp crackers, veggie straws.

column1: What are the two steps of freeze drying?
column2: (1) Freeze the food solid. (2) Dry it under vacuum (low pressure, low temperature) so the ice sublimes.

column1: What is sublimation?
column2: The change of a solid directly to vapour, skipping the liquid phase. In freeze drying, ice goes straight to water vapour.

column1: Sublimation appears twice in the course - as a defect and as a process. Where?
column2: As freeze burn (freezer burn) during frozen storage, and as the deliberate, controlled drying step in freeze drying.

column1: Why does freeze-dried food keep its original size and shape?
column2: Water leaves as vapour from wherever the ice crystals were, and each crystal leaves behind a void, so the structure never collapses.

column1: List the quality advantages of freeze-dried food.
column2: Keeps its original size and shape (an air-dried strawberry shrivels to about half size), keeps bright colour, rehydrates faster and better, and has excellent flavour and nutrient retention.

column1: What allows freeze-dried strawberries to stay bright pink?
column2: Low temperature drying under vacuum. No heat means no browning and no pigment damage - not added colourants.

column1: Air-dried vs freeze-dried strawberry: which rehydrates better and faster, and why?
column2: The freeze-dried one, because the voids left by sublimed ice crystals are open channels for water to rush back in.

column1: What are the disadvantages of freeze drying, and where is it used anyway?
column2: It is slow and expensive (freezing plus vacuum chambers). Used where quality justifies cost: premium instant coffee, astronaut food, camping meals.

column1: How do spray-dried and freeze-dried instant coffee differ in appearance?
column2: Spray dried is fine, dark and powdery; freeze dried is larger, lighter-coloured, glassy granules.

column1: What type of packaging material is best for dried foods, and why?
column2: Tin card (foil), because it blocks light and prevents oxidation. It is also a moisture barrier - hence the metallized lining of chip bags.

column1: Why do dried foods need protection from oxygen and light?
column2: They are high-surface-area products and are prone to oxidative rancidity; the package must also keep water out after all that water was removed.

column1: Why are plastic, cardboard, and glass not the best packaging for dried foods?
column2: Plastic alone is a decent water barrier but lets light through; cardboard prevents crushing but not moisture; glass appeals to consumers but does nothing useful here.

column1: Define the term "biotechnology".
column2: The use of living organisms, or parts of them, to make products. It covers both ancient fermentation (cheese, beer, soy sauce) and modern genetic engineering.

column1: Which one of the following was NOT a biotechnological (aka genetically modified) product: canola, cheese, insulin, or papaya?
column2: None of them - all four are biotechnology products. This is the classic "all of the above in disguise" answer.

column1: Give examples of biotechnology products named in Lesson 09.
column2: Beer, bovine rennin, flavouring ingredients, miso, soy sauce and xanthan gum - all of them. Also chymosin, vitamins, invertase, glutamic acid, bread, cheddar, yogurt and probiotic drinks (Yakult).

column1: Table 9.1: lactic acid bacteria acting on cucumbers, olives and cabbage give which fermented products?
column2: Cucumbers give dill pickles and sour pickles; olives give green olives and ripe olives; cabbage gives sauerkraut and kimchi.

column1: Table 9.1: lactic acid bacteria acting on milk, dairy and meat give which fermented products?
column2: Milk gives kishk; dairy gives sour cream and yogurt; meat gives meat sausages (salami).

column1: Which two "surprising" commodities in Table 9.1 are fermented by lactic acid bacteria?
column2: Coffee cherries (to coffee beans) and vanilla beans (to vanilla). Both pass through a fermentation step - a favourite exam curveball.

column1: Table 9.1: which microorganisms produce Swiss, Emmenthaler and Gruyere cheeses?
column2: Lactic acid bacteria together with propionic acid bacteria, acting on dairy products.

column1: Table 9.1: lactic acid bacteria with mould acting on vegetable products give what?
column2: Tempeh and soy sauce.

column1: Table 9.1: lactic acid bacteria with mould acting on dairy products give what?
column2: Roquefort, Camembert, Brie and blue cheeses.

column1: Table 9.1: list the yeast fermentations (commodity to product).
column2: Malt to beer, ale and stout; fruit to wine and vermouth; wines to brandy; rice to sake; bread dough to bread.

column1: Which microorganism leads to the production of alcoholic beverages, and how?
column2: Yeast; it converts glucose to ethanol. Not lactic acid bacteria, and not "ethanol to acetic acid" - that is the vinegar step.

column1: How is vinegar produced, and from which Table 9.1 commodity?
column2: Acetic acid bacteria acting on grapes; they convert the ethanol made by yeast into acetic acid. Two different organisms doing two separate steps.

column1: Name the three principles of preservation by fermentation.
column2: Microbial antagonism, antimicrobial agents, and lowering pH.

column1: What is microbial antagonism?
column2: It encourages the growth of alcohol- and acid-producing microorganisms while suppressing spoilage-causing microorganisms.

column1: What is a starter culture?
column2: The deliberate inoculation of the desired microorganisms - commercial yeast, a spoonful of yogurt, a sourdough starter - instead of relying on the right microbes arriving by chance.

column1: Which environmental factors must be controlled to create a favourable environment for fermentation?
column2: Temperature, salt, oxygen and moisture. Kimchi is the example: salt the cabbage, pack it tight to exclude oxygen, and hold it at the right temperature.

column1: Outline the full sequence of microbiological, chemical and physical changes converting milk to cheese.
column2: Pasteurize the milk; add the lactic acid culture (plus other microorganisms if chosen) and the coagulating enzyme (rennet or rennin-like substitute); fermentation converts lactose to lactic acid; curd coagulation as casein micelles form a gel; cutting and cooking; separation into curd and whey. The curd is then matted, milled, salted, pressed, cured and ripened, and packaged for retail.

column1: What is the key chemical change during the fermentation stage of cheese making?
column2: Lactic acid bacteria convert lactose to lactic acid, lowering the pH.

column1: What happens at the curd coagulation stage, and which two physical operations follow it?
column2: Casein micelles that are normally stable in calcium become calcium-sensitive micelles that form a gel. The gel is then cut and cooked, driving out liquid and splitting the mass into curd and whey.

column1: What is contained in the CURD?
column2: Casein, fat, most of the calcium and phosphorus, lactic acid, and water.

column1: What is contained in the WHEY?
column2: Whey proteins, water-soluble vitamins, some calcium and phosphorus, water, lactose, and lactic acid.

column1: After the curd is separated from the whey, what happens to it?
column2: It is matted, milled, salted, pressed, then cured and ripened, and finally packaged for retail.

column1: Why is whey a problem for the dairy industry?
column2: Whey disposal is a major problem faced by the dairy industry because of the high water and solids content of the whey.

column1: Name the enzyme responsible for cheese production and state where it is naturally found.
column2: Rennet, found in the 4th stomach of the calf (the abomasum). Chymosin is the active enzyme within rennet.

column1: What is the major function of rennet?
column2: Formation of a yoghurt-like coagulum - it curdles the milk. It does NOT convert lactose to lactic acid; that is the starter culture's job.

column1: How does industry obtain enough rennet without using calf stomachs?
column2: By genetic engineering: chymosin A is derived from Escherichia coli K-12, and chymosin B from Aspergillus niger or Kluyveromyces marxianus. Permitted cheese enzymes are listed in the Food and Drug Regulations, Division 8, B.08.033.

column1: How does genetically engineered chymosin appear in a cheese ingredient list?
column2: As "microbial enzyme" - e.g. pasteurized milk, salt, bacterial culture, calcium chloride, microbial enzyme.

column1: Give three major reasons for salting cheese.
column2: To draw the whey out of the curd, to flavour the final product, and to inhibit the growth of spoilage-causing microorganisms.

column1: What is NOT a major reason to salt cheese?
column2: To aid the functions of rennet and the starter culture. By the salting step their work is finished, and salt actually slows them down.

column1: Propionibacterium shermanii - which cheese, and what does it do?
column2: Swiss / Emmenthaler. It produces CO2 gas that forms the holes ("eyes") and gives a sweet, nutty flavour.

column1: Penicillium camembertii - which cheese, what does it hydrolyze, and what texture results?
column2: Camembert and Brie. It forms the white, velvet coating on the rind and hydrolyzes PROTEIN to give the creamy texture.

column1: Penicillium roquefortii - which cheese, what does it hydrolyze, and what appearance results?
column2: Roquefort and blue cheeses. It hydrolyzes MILK FAT, giving the blue-veined appearance and a sharp, piquant flavour.

column1: Which two regulatory agencies are responsible for regulating products derived from biotechnology in Canada?
column2: Health Canada and the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA). Not the WHO, the FAO or the Codex Alimentarius Commission.

column1: What are "novel foods" in Canada?
column2: All three of: (i) products that have never been used as a food, (ii) foods resulting from a process not previously used for food, and (iii) foods modified by genetic manipulation.

column1: What is the Canadian government's overall position on biotechnology-derived foods?
column2: Regulate by product, not by process - assess the safety of the food that actually results rather than banning a technique outright.

column1: What type of energy shown on the electromagnetic spectrum is used in our everyday cooking (e.g. a stove element)?
column2: Infrared. It is not microwave, ultraviolet, X-ray or gamma-ray.

column1: Where on the electromagnetic spectrum does food irradiation sit, and why is that region used?
column2: At the short-wavelength, high-energy end: gamma-rays and X-rays (ionizing energy). It is used because of its good penetration power through food and packaging.

column1: Name the three approved sources of ionizing energy for food irradiation.
column2:
1) Gamma radiation from Cobalt-60 or Cesium-137;
2) X-rays generated from a machine source at or below 5 MeV;
3) Electrons generated from a machine source at or below 10 MeV.

column1: What does the Gray (Gy; also kiloGray, kGy, or Rad) measure?
column2: The energy absorbed by a food, i.e. the irradiation dose.

column1: What is the maximum irradiation dose permitted in Canada?
column2: Less than 10 kGy.

column1: Describe the layout of a Cobalt-60 food irradiation facility.
column2: Cobalt-60 rods sit at the bottom of a water pool; food on an overhead conveyor passes above the source, absorbs the gamma rays, and moves on. The source never touches the food.

column1: What is the main regulatory concern in operating a food irradiation facility?
column2: The safety of the personnel operating the plant, not the safety of the food.

column1: What are the two mechanisms by which ionizing energy preserves food?
column2:
Direct effect: damage to DNA materials.
Indirect effect: formation of free radicals and hydrogen peroxide from water.

column1: List the six consequences of the DIRECT DNA damage caused by ionizing energy.
column2: (i) Destruction of microorganisms, (ii) destruction of insects, (iii) inactivation of parasites, (iv) delaying of ripening, (v) sprouting inhibition, (vi) destruction of enzymes. The answer is All of them.

column1: Why do irradiated potatoes and onions not sprout?
column2: The direct DNA damage hits the still-living food tissue, giving sprouting inhibition and delayed ripening.

column1: Ionizing energy preserves food INDIRECTLY by forming what?
column2: Free radicals, hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), and radiolytic products, which attack microbial cells chemically.

column1: Is 'radiative food' (radioactive food) formed by the indirect effect of irradiation?
column2: No. Free radicals, hydrogen peroxide and radiolytic products are formed, but the food does not become radioactive.

column1: Radicidation: what dose and what target?
column2: Less than 10 kGy; destroys disease-causing (pathogenic) microorganisms.

column1: Radurization: what dose and what target?
column2: Less than 10 kGy; destroys spoilage-causing microorganisms.

column1: Radappertization: what dose and what target?
column2: Greater than 10 kGy; achieves sterilization. Named after Appert, the father of canning.

column1: Which irradiation terminology is analogous to pasteurization, and which to commercial sterilization?
column2: Radicidation is analogous to pasteurization; radappertization is analogous to commercial sterilization.

column1: Which of the three irradiation treatments could NOT be approved in Canada, and why?
column2: Radappertization, because it requires more than 10 kGy and Canada's limit is less than 10 kGy.

column1: Define the D-value as used for ionizing energy.
column2: The absorbed energy dosage that produces a decimal reduction (90% reduction) of the targeted microbial population. It is expressed in kGy rather than minutes.

column1: For irradiation, how many decimal reductions are required for acid foods versus low-acid foods?
column2: Acid foods 5D; low-acid foods 12D.

column1: A manufacturer wants to irradiate FoodABC; the target organism's D-value is 0.9 kGy. Will the process be approved?
column2: It depends on the pH of the product. Acid food: 5D = 4.5 kGy (under the limit); low-acid food: 12D = 10.8 kGy (over Canada's 10 kGy limit).

column1: Public concern: does irradiated food become radioactive?
column2: No. Exposure is low and the energy is below 10 MeV, too low to induce radioactivity in the food.

column1: Public concern: what are the by-products of irradiation called?
column2: Unique radiolytic products. They occur in tiny amounts and many are the same compounds produced by ordinary cooking.

column1: List the three precautionary steps used to minimize irradiation damage to food.
column2: Irradiating frozen foods, irradiating in vacuum, and adding free radical scavengers.

column1: Why irradiate food frozen, why under vacuum, and what are free radical scavengers?
column2: Frozen: less free water means fewer free radicals. Vacuum: no oxygen for oxidation. Scavengers are antioxidants such as vitamins C and E that mop up free radicals.

column1: Which agency is responsible for the labelling and advertising of irradiated foods in Canada?
column2: The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA), under Division 16 of the Food and Drug Regulations.

column1: What is the role of the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission in food irradiation?
column2: It regulates the uses of the radiation sources.

column1: What is the role of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited (AECL) in food irradiation?
column2: It develops the irradiators. It is not the labelling agency.

column1: Which foods are approved for irradiation in Canada?
column2: Potatoes, onion, wheat and wheat flour, dried spices, and ground beef (approved in 2017). Five items.

column1: How does the list of foods approved for irradiation in Canada compare with that of the US?
column2: Canada's list is short (five items); the US has approved a far longer list of foods for irradiation.

column1: What must appear on the label of an irradiated food?
column2: A statement - 'treated by irradiation', 'treated with radiation', or 'irradiated' - plus the radura symbol, the green stylized plant in a broken circle.

column1: When must an irradiated ingredient be declared as 'irradiated' in the ingredient list of another food?
column2: Only if the irradiated ingredient constitutes 10% or more of the final food.

column1: A frozen turkey dinner contains irradiated dried spices at about 1% of total weight. How must the irradiation be declared?
column2: It does not have to be declared at all, because the irradiated ingredient is less than 10% of the final food.

column1: Is a hazard symbol part of Canadian irradiation labelling?
column2: No. Only the statement (e.g. 'treated by irradiation') and the radura symbol are required; there is no hazard symbol.

column1: Where are Canada's irradiated food processing facilities located?
column2: Port Coquitlam, British Columbia and Laval, Quebec. None are on any UBC campus.

column1: List the benefits (advantages) of food processing.
column2: Food safety; year-round availability regardless of season or climate; longer shelf life; convenience; less waste; and improved bioavailability of nutrients.

column1: List the risks (disadvantages) of food processing, and the framing caveat about raw foods.
column2:
Risks: loss of some nutrients (especially heat- and water-sensitive vitamins) and changes in flavour, colour and texture.
Caveat: raw foods vary widely in nutrient content (genetics, climate, soil, ripeness) sometimes as much as or more than processing changes them.

column1: Deck quiz: Processing increases the bioavailability of nutrients by destroying which of the following? (amylase inhibitors / thiaminase / avidin)
column2: All of the above. Heat processing destroys all three antinutritional (antidigestive) factors.

column1: Where are trypsin and amylase inhibitors found, and what does heat processing do to them?
column2: Found in cereal grains, peas and beans. Heat destroys these antidigestive factors, improving the bioavailability (digestibility) of the proteins and carbohydrates in these products.

column1: What is thiaminase, where is it found, and why does heat processing matter?
column2: An enzyme that destroys thiamin (vitamin B1); found in fish, shellfish, brussels sprouts and red cabbage. Heat processing destroys it, sparing the thiamin.

column1: What does avidin do, where is it found, and what destroys it?
column2: Avidin (with other factors in raw egg white) binds biotin and some of the iron present in egg yolk, making these nutrients biologically unavailable. Heat processing destroys it.

column1: Besides destroying antinutritional factors, name the other positive nutritional effects of heat processing.
column2: Increases digestibility of starch (gelatinization) and protein (denaturation); increases bioavailability of niacin, which is present in many cereals in a bound form; increases palatability, giving greater appeal and nutrient consumption.

column1: Deck quiz: Which nutrient is MOST stable under thermal processing - carbohydrates, protein, fat, vitamins or minerals?
column2: Minerals. Vitamins are the fragile group; minerals can leach into cooking water but do not degrade.

column1: Deck quiz: Which vitamin is LEAST stable at normal food pH (below pH 7) - A, C or E?
column2: Vitamin A. In Table 2 vitamin A is unstable in acid, while vitamins C and E are stable in acid.

column1: Table 2: give the full stability profile of vitamin C.
column2: Unstable at neutral pH, in alkali, in air/oxygen, in light and in heat. Stable only in acid (pH below 7).

column1: Table 2: give the stability profile of vitamin A and beta-carotene.
column2: Both are unstable in acid, in air/oxygen, in light and in heat. Both are stable at neutral pH.

column1: Table 2: give the stability profiles of vitamin E and riboflavin.
column2: Vitamin E is unstable in air/oxygen, light and heat (stable across pH). Riboflavin is notably unstable in light - which is why milk is not sold in clear glass.

column1: Table 2: give the stability profile of thiamin (B1).
column2: Unstable in alkali and in heat; stable in acid. It is the weakest of the thiamin/niacin/pyridoxine trio.

column1: Learning objective: compare and contrast the stability of (a) vitamins A, C and E versus (b) thiamin (B1), niacin (B2) and pyridoxine (B6).
column2: A, C and E are the vulnerable group - readily destroyed by oxygen, light and heat (plus acid for A, and everything but acid for C). Thiamin, niacin and pyridoxine are the comparatively stable group, with niacin the most stable and thiamin the weakest of the three.

column1: Table 3: percentage nutrient losses from blanching in water versus with steam, and why they differ.
column2:
Water: vitamin C 16-58%, riboflavin 30-50%, thiamin 16-34%, niacin 32-37%.
Steam: vitamin C only 16-26%, vitamin B6 21% - steam retains more because water-soluble vitamins leach out into the blanching water.

column1: Table 4: percentage nutrient losses from conventional canning of vegetables.
column2: Vitamin C 33-90%; thiamin 16-83%; riboflavin 25-67%; niacin 0-75%; folacin 35-84%; pantothenic acid 30-85%; vitamin B6 0-91%; biotin 0-78%; vitamin A 0-84%.
